blocks.text: Walk past a *kahvehane*, a neighbourhood coffeehouse, on almost any afternoon and you will hear it before you see it: the rattle of dice on wood and the click of tiles. Inside, at small tables, people sit over glasses of tea and play *tavla* (backgammon), *okey* or cards, while friends look on and comment on every move.

Coffeehouses have been part of Turkish town life since the first ones opened in Istanbul in the 1550s (see [Turkish coffee](a1-u12-culture)). The 17th-century historian Peçuylu İbrahim already noted that some of their customers played backgammon and chess. By the 19th century most neighbourhood coffeehouses stood beside the local mosque, and a new kind appeared, the *kıraathane* or reading room, which kept newspapers and magazines for its customers; the first, Sarafim's, opened on Divanyolu in Istanbul in 1857. Many coffeehouses still write *kıraathane* on their signs, though today their customers order far more tea than coffee.

*Tavla* belongs to the family of board games that includes backgammon: a board of 24 points, 15 pieces for each player, two dice. The earliest game of this kind that can be clearly identified is the Roman and Byzantine *tabula*, known from a Greek epigram about a game played by the emperor Zeno in the 5th century. Its name lives on in the Italian *tavola*, which gave Turkish *tavla*.

The pieces are called *pul* and the dice *zar*. Players call the numbers on the dice by their old Persian names: *yek* (1), *dü* (2), *se* (3), *cihar* (4), *penç* (5) and *şeş* (6). A roll of six and five is *şeşbeş*, and a double six is *düşeş*, from Persian **two sixes**. The word has left the board: in everyday Turkish a *düşeş* is a lucky surprise, such as an unexpected and welcome visit.

*Okey* is a game of the rummy family played with 106 tiles: the numbers 1 to 13 in four colours, two of each, and two false jokers. Usually four people play. Each sets 14 tiles on a wooden rack (one player starts with 15) and tries to arrange them into runs and sets, drawing one tile and discarding one at each turn. A tile turned face up at the start, the *gösterge* or indicator, decides which tile will be the wild *okey* of that round. The set is the same as that of Rummikub, and okey is played as much at home, at family gatherings, as in the coffeehouse.
Here is a grandfather's day, in the aorist of this unit:

blocks.tr: Dedem her sabah kahvehaneye gider. Orada arkadaşlarıyla çay içer, gazete okur ve tavla oynar. Zarları atar ve “Şeşbeş!” der. Bazen kazanır, bazen kaybeder. Ama akşam eve döner ve her zaman “Bugün ben kazandım!” der. Babaannem ona hiç inanmaz.
blocks.en: My grandfather goes to the coffeehouse every morning. There he drinks tea with his friends, reads the paper and plays backgammon. He throws the dice and calls out “Six-five!” Sometimes he wins, sometimes he loses. But in the evening he comes home and always says, “I won today!” My grandmother never believes him.

questions.q: Where does the name *tavla* come from?
options: the name of a coffeehouse in Istanbul
questions.explain: *Tabula* (board) was the Roman and Byzantine game; Italian *tavola* gave Turkish *tavla*.

questions.q: What does the *gösterge* tile decide in okey?
options: which tile is the wild okey
how many tiles each player gets

questions.q: In the Turkish text, what does the grandfather say every evening?
questions.explain: *Her zaman “Bugün ben kazandım!” der*, and the grandmother never believes him.

sources.title: Kahvehane
sources.note: First Istanbul coffeehouses in the early 1550s (Tahtakale, 1554–1555, after Peçuylu İbrahim, who notes customers playing tavla and chess); 19th-century neighbourhood coffeehouses beside mosques; the kıraathane from the Tanzimat period, the first being Sarafim Kıraathanesi on Divanyolu in 1857

sources.title: Kahvehane
sources.note: The same dates; games of tavla and chess; kıraathanes with newspapers and magazines; tea spreading from the late 19th century

sources.title: Backgammon
sources.note: Tabula as the earliest identifiable tables game, described in an epigram of the emperor Zeno (476–491), with 24 points and 15 pieces per player; Turkish names of rolls (şeş beş, dü şeş, hep yek)

sources.title: tavla, düşeş, şeşbeş, cihar, penç
sources.note: tavla from Italian tavola, a game of 15 pieces per player and two dice; düşeş from Persian dū + şeş, also figuratively an unexpected but welcome encounter or visit; şeşbeş a roll of six and five; cihar (four) and penç (five) from Persian

sources.title: Okey
sources.note: A rummy-family tile game popular in Turkey; 106 tiles, 1 to 13, two false jokers; usually four players with 14 tiles (15 for the first player); the face-up indicator tile sets the joker

sources.title: Rummikub
sources.note: 106 tiles in four colours, two of each number from 1 to 13, and two jokers; in Turkey a variant called okey is widely played by families at gatherings and in local cafés
